How this report was built — and where to be careful

Read this before quoting figures from this report. The talks below were reconstructed from a phone's live-translation screenshots (Flitto's real-time English captioning of Korean and English speech) and photos of presentation screens, not an official transcript. That means:
  • Numbers and quotes are the speakers' claims, relayed through machine translation — treat every statistic as "cited by the speaker," not independently verified by us.
  • Some sentences are cut off where a floating "New messages" button covered the caption feed, or where a photo was blurry or cropped. Gaps are not filled in with guesses.
  • A few names have uncertain spelling in the live captions (flagged inline as e.g. name unconfirmed) and should be verified against the official program before being used in citations or outreach.
  • On-site signage read "Aug 19–21, 2026," a three-day range, but the source material only covers two days of sessions (Aug 19 and Aug 20) — worth reconciling against the official agenda if a third day's content turns up later.

Day 1 — Foundations & the enterprise reality check

The first day moved from where agentic AI came from, to how far it actually reaches into production today — with two recurring warnings: most AI pilots never scale past a demo, and the physical/robotics wave ("Physical AI") is arriving faster than the safety testing built for it.

Morning · Main Stage

The Long Road to Agentic AI: A Pioneer's Perspective 선구자의 관점에서 본 AI 어시스턴트에서 에이전틱 AI의 시대

Speaker name not captured on slide Career: SRI → Nuance → Yahoo → Cortana → Google Assistant → Samsung Bixby/Viv → Georgia Tech
  • Traced "agentic AI" back to SRI's 1995 Office Assistant — a facilitator agent routing speech, email, and calendar requests across specialist agents, the direct ancestor of Siri and of what we now call tool-calling and multi-agent orchestration.
  • Argued 2010s-era assistants (Cortana, Google Assistant, Bixby) had a real "belief state" and dialogue policy governing every action — deliberately constrained, but controllable and repairable.
  • Called 2022's ChatGPT moment "the wrong turn": fluent, but the belief state, policy, and repair mechanisms of the old architecture were discarded along with the friction.
  • Cited 2026 research showing today's agents guess through ambiguity (89% success with a clarified task vs. 6.7% with an ambiguous one) and anchor on their own wrong assumptions across multi-turn conversations.
  • Proposed fixing this with a much smaller "sidecar" controller reading the model's internal state (not the transcript) plus multimodal, real-time repair — "a meeting of the minds," not more autonomy.
TakeawayFluency is not the same as reliability. The field spent a decade building controllable dialogue systems, then reset to something less steerable when LLMs arrived — the fix on offer is smaller, checkable control layers, not bigger models.
Morning · Main Stage

Agentic AI in Space: Traditional and Agentic AI Are Revolutionizing Space 지구 밖의 자율 AI: 60개 위성이 스스로 생각하고 협력하는 법

Speaker name not captured on slide
  • Demoed a workflow across roughly 60 satellites that autonomously detects an event (e.g. a volcanic thermal signature), tasks the right sensors among available satellites, and tracks it — illustrated live with a simulated Mount Pinatubo eruption plume (confirmed via the session's audio recording).
  • Framed the goal as "humans on the loop, not in the loop" — humans set intent and review outcomes; the system handles fulfillment and micro-management.
  • Closed on "generalist workflow generation" — moving from hand-built pipelines per mission to agents that assemble a workflow from the goal itself.
TakeawayThe "on-the-loop" framing — set the goal, review the outcome, let the system handle orchestration — is a clean design pattern for any multi-sensor / multi-system monitoring problem, on Earth or off it.
Morning · Main Stage

Is AI Actually Helping Enterprise Productivity?

Featuring Prof. Kyungjong Lee — KB Kookmin Bank / KB Financial Group
  • Opened with a sobering statistic: of executives running multiple AI projects, only 6% report the projects moved net profit by more than 2% — 94% saw no measurable financial impact.
  • Cited a Bank of Korea / National Information Society Agency joint survey: 60–70% of Korean companies say they're adopting AI, but fewer than 10% report actual results.
  • Referenced Gartner data that over 50% of enterprise AI projects are discontinued at the proof-of-concept stage.
  • Prof. Kyungjong Lee described KB Financial Group's own agentic-AI platform: development began in 2024, the platform launched April 2025, with full-scale AI agent development following.
TakeawayAdoption and results are two different numbers, and the gap between them is the story of 2026 — a theme that returned in nearly every later session (DeepMind's "80% never reach production," the Woori/LG panel's "who presses the button" problem).
Midday · Main Stage

2026 Enterprise Agentic AX Technology Trends: Harness & Loop Engineering 2026 Enterprise Agentic AX 기술 트렌드 및 Harness & Loop 엔지니어링 적용 사례 소개

Speaker name not captured on slide
  • Named the emerging discipline stack: Prompt → Context → Harness → Loop → Graph Engineering, each layer solving what the previous one couldn't scale.
  • Harness Engineering (5 levels shown): from casual ChatGPT use (L1), to local CLI tools like Claude Code / Codex (L2), to multi-tool agent platforms (L3), to full pro-code harnesses with governance guardrails at enterprise grade (L5). "High freedom, hard to control" was the explicit warning about the low-governance end of that ladder.
  • Loop Engineering (citing Addy Osmani): "you design the system that prompts the agent" — a 5-step loop of set goal → agent executes → agent verifies → fix on failure → finish on pass, with a human "on the loop" for long-term trajectory.
  • Covered long-term memory architecture options (mem0, Graphiti, Palantir Foundry's ontology layers) as the piece agentic systems still lack by default.
  • Closed on the "FDE (Forward-Deployed Engineer) Layer" land-grab: Anthropic ($1.5B enterprise AI services venture with Wall Street), OpenAI ($4B+ deployment company), AWS ($1B forward-deployed engineers), and Microsoft Frontier Company ($2.5B, 6,000 embedded experts) are all racing to own the "last mile" of enterprise AI deployment.
TakeawayEvery major AI vendor is now selling the deployment layer, not just the model — a $9B+ market of "forward-deployed engineers" says the hard part was never picking a model, it's the harness and governance around it.
Afternoon · Main Stage

The Agentic Data Stack: Speed and Simplicity for AI That Scales

ClickHouse
  • Walked the 2022–2025 timeline from LLMs → RAG → AI agents → reasoning models, arguing each step increased how many, and how unpredictably, a system queries its own database.
  • Contrasted "classic" real-time analytics (one predictable query path per user request) with "agentic" analytics (an agent layer fanning out many concurrent, unpredictable queries against the same database).
  • Cited OpenAI's and Anthropic's own use of ClickHouse for petabyte-scale observability — OpenAI ingests log volume compared to "500 Libraries of Congress a day," growing 20%+ per month; Anthropic's Maruth Goyal credited ClickHouse as instrumental in shipping Claude 4.
TakeawayAgents don't just need "a database" — they need one built for many unpredictable concurrent queries, not the one predictable query path traditional applications assume.
Afternoon · Main Stage

From Models to Reality: What It Takes to Run AI Reliably at Scale 모델에서 현실까지: 대규모 AI를 안정적으로 운영하기 위한 조건

Colin Presly · VP, Customer Engineering, Seagate Technology
  • Framed AI maturity as three stages — Exploration ("can we build useful models?") → Deployment ("can we run this in production?") → Scale ("does it create lasting value?") — and placed most enterprises still crossing from stage one to two.
  • Cited IDC data on data growth: <1 zettabyte generated in 2005, 72 ZB in 2020, a projected 527 ZB by 2029 — and argued AI training and inference create two different, both-growing demand curves (training: bursty/archival; inference: persistent/compounding).
  • Presented an AI storage reference architecture where 85–95% of all AI data ultimately rests on hard drives, not GPU memory or SSD cache — positioning storage density (via Seagate's HAMR-based "Mozaic" 44TB drives) as a direct lever on AI infrastructure cost and carbon footprint.
TakeawayEvery AI roadmap conversation eventually becomes a storage and data-governance conversation — model choice gets the attention, but where and how the data lives decides whether the model can be trusted or afforded at scale.
Afternoon · Main Stage

How AI Is Redefining the Future of Work AI가 바꾸는 일의 미래

Speaker name not captured on slide
  • Opened with workforce composition: roughly 30% of the global office workforce is now Gen Z, with notably higher rates of side-business planning and entrepreneurial intent than prior cohorts.
  • Noted Korea-specific context: mandatory military service and extended job-preparation periods push back the age Korean Gen Z workers actually start full-time roles, compared to other markets.
TakeawayThe workforce adopting AI tools fastest is also the newest and least tenured — governance and training programs built only for senior staff will miss where AI habits are actually forming first.
Late afternoon · Keynote

Building as a Creative Act: An Innovator's Mindset for the AI Age AI 시대의 혁신가의 마인드셋

Savannah Kunovsky · Managing Director, IDEO AI MTechLab
  • Opening keynote of the afternoon block, introduced explicitly as a lecture on "the innovator's mindset in the age of AI" from IDEO's AI-focused lab.
  • Her framing of embodiment — AI's move from the screen into the physical, sensed world — was picked up directly by name in the Physical AI panel later that day as a working definition to react to.
Takeaway"Embodiment" — not just intelligence, but intelligence that has to act in and be checked against a physical world — was this summit's connective thread between design thinking and hard robotics/defense discussions.
Late afternoon · Main Stage

Beyond Better Models: What Will Define the Next Era of AI? AI 에이전트의 미래: 더 나은 모델이 아니라 더 나은 워크플로우

Genspark
  • Shared growth figures for context, not boasting: $250M ARR in 12 months from zero, $645M raised at a $2.6B valuation, 7,000+ business customers "actually running the system."
  • Core thesis: "better models will keep shipping — the breakthrough is context." Sketched a "second brain" style context layer that follows the person across apps rather than living inside any one model or tool.
TakeawayA second vendor independently arrived at the same conclusion as the morning's "Pioneer's Perspective" talk: the unlock is a persistent context/memory layer around the model, not a bigger model.
Evening · Keynote Panel

The Era of Physical AI: The Future of Industry Transformed by Physical AI

Moderator: Prof. Doohee Jeong — Handong Global University / Impactive AI Prof. Ahyoung Kim — Seoul National University Tony Jang — CEO, FactoryLab.AI (ex-Hyundai AutoEver) CTO Seung-young Lee — LIG Defense & Aerospace
  • Why now: Prof. Kim traced the inflection point through AlphaGo → a CNN-based era that disappointed robotics (2014–2020) → the Transformer, which succeeded in language (GPT), then vision, then robotics — the shift from sensing to actually understanding what's sensed.
  • Demo vs. mass production, three tests (Tony Jang): does adopting it require changing the existing system (→ demo, if yes)? does failure fit inside the intended cycle time? is the data needed for retraining clearly defined? All three "yes" is when something is real, not a "cool demo."
  • World models, real or marketing (Tony Jang): a simulator with real physics (their own "Dreamer") is proven technology; a model claiming to perfectly understand physics from scratch is "still at the packaging stage." Cited a described Tesla Optimus incident — misidentifying a coworker as a part and pinning them to a wall — as the cost of getting this wrong.
  • Where autonomy should stop (CTO Seung-young Lee, defense context): the deciding line is irreversibility, not capability. Where a decision is irreversible, AI's role is to hand humans better information faster, not to decide — a deliberate boundary, not a technical limit.
  • The lab-to-field gap (Prof. Kim): roughly 50/50 software (the "sim-to-real gap" — lab lighting/noise conditions don't transfer) vs. hardware (real heat, vibration, and comms degradation that's hard to simulate at all).
  • Safety under active adversaries (CTO Lee): in defense, "noise" isn't the threat model — deliberate deception and jamming are. His answer: build a test distribution, not fixed test cases, covering realistic variable ranges (e.g. wave height 0–5m, jamming-degraded comms as a probability range), continuously widened with new edge cases, in a closed loop with real-world results — and treat this as needing state/regulatory involvement, not something one company solves alone.
TakeawayThe panel's most exportable idea: use irreversibility, not technical capability, as the line for how much autonomy any AI system gets — and verify a physical AI system against a distribution of realistic conditions, not a fixed checklist, before trusting it in the field.
Evening · Main Stage

The Rise of AI-Native Work AI 네이티브 워크플로우 혁명

Laurent Thevenet — Head of Creative Technology, APAC & MEA, Publicis Groupe
  • "Instant capability ≠ expertise": capability gives you output, expertise gives you judgment about what's good and what can go wrong — "the gap is slop."
  • Warned against "tokenmaxxing" as a substitute for transformation — routing the right model to the right task is infrastructure, not strategy.
  • Argued the answer to ungoverned tool sprawl isn't restricting builders, but giving them a shared, open internal ecosystem (core infra, core tools, core data) to plug into.
  • Proposed ownership must scale with adoption: 5 users → a builder owns it; 50 users → needs a named product owner; 500 users → needs a full product team.
TakeawayThe ownership ladder (5 → builder, 50 → product owner, 500 → product team) is a ready-made rule of thumb for exactly when an internal AI prototype needs to graduate into something formally governed.

Day 2 — Industry deployment & governance

The second day shifted from "what is agentic AI" to "why doesn't it work yet at our scale" — data debt, change management, and the uncomfortable question of who is willing to press the button on a rollout.

Morning · Main Stage

The Conditions for AX Success and a Truly AI-Native Enterprise

Speaker name not captured on slide
  • Presented a 2×2 "agentic maturity" model (Levels 1–4) for scoring how far an organization's AI use has actually progressed, from occasional tool use toward genuine agentic workflows.
Captured only in slide/photo form; the live-caption detail for this specific talk was not fully recovered from the source images.
Morning · Track A

Accelerating Breakthroughs with AI: Unlocking Opportunities in Traditional Industries

Ramine Tinati — Head of APAC, Google DeepMind Moderator: Seri Kim
  • Opened with DeepMind's science-first origin story (AlphaGo's 2016 match played in Seoul), then its track record outside chatbots: AlphaFold (200M+ protein structures, now free including commercial use), GNOME (2.2M predicted crystal structures for materials science), and WeatherNext/WeatherNext Cyclone forecasting.
  • Central stat: roughly 80% of AI implementations never reach full production at scale — framed as a systems problem spanning people, data, existing systems, and infrastructure, not a model-quality problem.
  • Why pilots stall — 3 causes: data debt & silos, workflow disconnect (AI bolted on as a standalone tool instead of embedded in daily operations), and cultural/operating inertia (rigid hierarchy, no executive ownership).
  • Four pillars to overcome it: data foundations (semantic grounding in verified enterprise data), domain adaptation (continuous evaluation against industry terminology), agentic workflow integration (moving beyond chat into embedded task execution), governance & safety (deterministic validation, guardrails).
  • Named three "untapped frontier" industries for this approach: life sciences & biotech, manufacturing & supply chain, telecom & critical infrastructure.
TakeawayThe most cited number of the summit — 80% of AI implementations don't reach production — has a consistent root cause across every speaker who addressed it: data readiness and workflow embedding, not model capability.
Morning · Main Stage

The Present and Future of Payment in the Age of AI AI 기술과 만난 결제(Payment)의 현재와 미래

Sunghee An — Executive Director, Shinhan Card AX Research Institute
  • Mapped the competitive landscape of AI-in-payments across four player types: AI platforms partnering into payments (OpenAI + Stripe, Google), operator-native wallets (KakaoPay, NaverPay, Samsung Pay), e-commerce platforms (Amazon, Walmart), and payment networks (Mastercard, Visa).
  • Introduced Shinhan's own "Agent Pay" pilot — AI agents initiating or managing payments on a customer's behalf.
TakeawayPayments is a preview of what's coming to every regulated, trust-sensitive workflow: general AI platforms, incumbent operators, and network players are all racing to put an agent in the same transaction loop.
Midday · Main Stage

Decisions vs. Tasks: What Agentic AI Actually Means in Operations

Prent Mishra
  • Captured via stage/slide photos only; the live-caption detail for this talk's argument was not fully recovered from the source images, beyond the session's framing distinction between automating discrete tasks versus delegating actual decisions.
Flagged for follow-up if a fuller transcript or recording becomes available — the distinction it's built around (task automation vs. decision delegation) is directly relevant to the governance recommendations below.
Afternoon · Track D

Panel: Hidden Bottlenecks in Enterprise AI — Data Quality, Governance, and Reality

Moderator: name unconfirmed ("Seunghyun"/"Seunghwan" Lee), VP, Samil PwC Yongmin Choi — Head of AI Strategy Center, Woori Financial Group Yoonhee Hwang — Senior VP, Data Intelligence, LG Electronics
  • Named the biggest bottleneck of the past 2–3 years not as technology or even data itself, but the moment someone senior has to "press the button" to scale a proven PoC — described as the single largest obstacle to enterprise-wide adoption.
  • Used a Gold Rush analogy: in past waves, the money went to the infrastructure sellers (Samsung Electronics, NVIDIA, TSMC), not most of the prospectors — a caution against over-investing in compute before proving workflow value.
  • Cited Jensen Huang's framing that the future IT department becomes "the HR department for AI agents" — and debated openly whether AI agents should be managed as software accounts or as digital employees with defined roles and permissions.
  • LG Electronics' Yoonhee Hwang described running Customer Data Platforms across 30+ countries and the specific difficulty of scaling a working Text-to-SQL PoC into production: as more tables and metadata are added, the retrieval context grows faster than the model's context window, and PoC-level accuracy quietly degrades in production.
  • Closing recommendation: pair every AI rollout with a Process Innovation (PI) redesign and a re-assignment of roles & responsibilities (R&R) — not just "add AI to the existing process."
TakeawayExecutive risk-aversion, not data or model quality, was named as the single largest bottleneck in this panel — a governance and incentive problem more than a technical one.
Afternoon · Track D

Panel: AI Governance in Manufacturing

Three panelists, names not captured in the recovered transcript
  • Framed the core difficulty as converting tacit, siloed departmental knowledge into shared data before any agent can act on it — "the challenge of how to turn tacit knowledge into data, and how to reach a consensus on creating a shared perspective within an organization."
  • Raised competitive-cost pressure directly (anonymized as "Brand J," "Brand C") and the practical difficulty of hiring skilled on-site talent internationally, as reasons manufacturers are turning to agentic tooling for field operations.
  • Referenced Palantir's "Forward-Deployed Engineer" (FDE) organizational role as a capability every enterprise doing this work will eventually need internally, regardless of which vendor's platform it uses.
  • Closed with a candid framing: as agents absorb roughly half a team's prior workload, the point isn't to eliminate the team — it's to redeploy them to work the tools were never suited for.
Takeaway"Turning tacit knowledge into data" is the unglamorous, unavoidable first step before any manufacturing AI agent can be trusted — no vendor platform substitutes for that internal groundwork.
Afternoon · Main Stage

Agentic AI Strategies for Building Digital Resilience 디지털 레질리언스 구축을 위한 에이전틱 AI 전략

Cisco
  • Presented a "Data Fabric" architecture routing machine data (via Splunk) into a low-cost Machine Data Lake, then branching into ML training, compliance, security monitoring, incident response, observability, and generative-AI/agent use cases from one shared foundation.
  • Positioned this shared data layer as the prerequisite for reliable AI/agent operations and automated incident response — echoing the data-foundations pillar from the DeepMind talk earlier.
TakeawayDigital resilience and AI-agent readiness are converging on the same requirement: one well-governed data/telemetry layer that every downstream use case draws from, instead of a separate pipeline per tool.
Late afternoon · Track A

From Intuition to Intelligence: How AI Has Redefined Revenue Growth 세일즈 과학의 혁명: AI는 영업을 어떻게 바꼈는가

Barra Ó Briain — Head of APEC Sales, Gong
  • Cited PwC (Apr. 2026): 74% of AI's economic value is captured by just 20% of organizations — not because they bought more software, but because they redesigned workflows around it and let AI make more decisions (while investing in more governance, not less).
  • Contrasted McKinsey's 88% AI-adoption figure with Gartner's finding that 60% of AI initiatives are on track to miss their intended outcomes — "everyone has the tool, almost no one has the value."
  • Proposed a formula for what an AI outcome actually is: Efficiency × Effectiveness = Productivity — most organizations chase efficiency (automating tasks) and stop there, skipping the harder effectiveness half.
  • From analysis of millions of real sales calls: top-performing reps talk ~46% of the time vs. ~68% for average reps and ~72% for the bottom tier; top reps also wait until minute 38–46 of a call before discussing price ("value first, price late").
  • Cited customer outcomes: ~10 hours per rep returned weekly, ~46–50% reduction in new-hire ramp time, and a customer-quoted 64% productivity increase — with Anthropic named as one customer using the platform.
Takeaway"Efficiency × Effectiveness = Productivity" is a simple, reusable litmus test for whether an AI deployment is actually improving outcomes, or just automating the easy half of the job.

03

Cross-cutting themes

Read across all 21 sessions, four ideas kept resurfacing regardless of industry or track.

01

Most AI pilots die before production — and it's rarely the model's fault

From the morning enterprise-productivity talk (94% see no profit impact) to DeepMind's "80% never reach production" to the Woori/LG panel's "who presses the button" problem: data debt, workflow disconnect, and executive risk-aversion were named as the real blockers across at least five separate sessions, on three different tracks.

02

The deployment layer is the new battleground, not the model

Harness Engineering's five levels, the $9B+ "FDE Layer" land-grab among Anthropic/OpenAI/AWS/Microsoft, and Publicis's "tokenmaxxing ≠ transformation" all point the same way: picking a model is now the easy part; the harness, governance, and human-ownership structure around it is where projects succeed or stall.

03

Physical AI needs a different safety bar than software AI

The Physical AI panel's "irreversibility, not capability" boundary, and its "test a distribution, not a checklist" answer to safety verification, echoed in the manufacturing panel's caution about siloed knowledge and in Seagate's storage-reliability framing — the moment an AI acts in the physical world, its failure mode changes from "wrong answer" to "accident."

04

Data readiness is the prerequisite everyone independently converged on

ClickHouse (unpredictable concurrent agent queries), Seagate (85–95% of AI data lives on cold storage), DeepMind (data foundations as pillar one of four), Cisco (one shared data fabric feeding every downstream use case), and the manufacturing panel ("turn tacit knowledge into data" first) all named the same prerequisite in different words.

04

What this means for the La Salle System

Mapped against what's already true of TOIC's app fleet at De La Salle Lipa and DLS-CSB's accreditation/QMS work at Benilde — not generic AI advice, but the summit's specific ideas applied to work already underway.

1 · Treat every new AI feature as a pilot until it clears the "three tests," not a rollout

from: Physical AI panel · DeepMind

Why it matters here: TOIC already runs ~30+ Apps Script systems and is actively adding AI touch-points (We Help chatbot, AI Roadmap Phase 1's "AI suggests, humans approve" integrations for 2027). The summit's single most repeated warning — most pilots never clear production — argues for a formal go/no-go gate before any AI feature ships broadly, not after.

Do next
  • Adopt Tony Jang's three-part test for any new AI feature before wider rollout: does it need the existing system changed? does its failure fit inside the process's normal cycle time? is its retraining/monitoring data clearly owned?
  • Add a written go/no-go checkpoint to the AI Roadmap's Phase 1 integrations, gated on those three answers.
Watch for
  • A feature that "works in the demo" but needs a workaround, an exception, or a manual override to fit into TOIC's actual workflows — that's the "cool demo, not mass production" pattern almost every speaker warned about.

2 · Use "irreversibility," not capability, as the line for what AI is allowed to decide

from: Physical AI panel

Why it matters here: This maps cleanly onto the AI Roadmap's existing HITL (human-in-the-loop) anchor. It gives that principle a concrete test: not "is a human generally involved," but "can this specific decision be undone if the AI is wrong." Turnstile/access-control decisions, device-inventory write-offs, and student-facing communications sit at different points on that scale — and should be governed differently.

Do next
  • Classify current and planned AI touch-points (We Help chatbot, device inventory automation, any future turnstile/CDAP logic) by reversibility, not by how "smart" the feature is.
  • For anything irreversible — access denial, a flagged safety incident, a financial approval — keep AI in an advisory role only: it surfaces information, a person decides.
Watch for
  • Scope creep: a feature that started as "AI suggests" quietly becoming "AI decides" as staff learn to trust it — worth an explicit annual review, not just an initial approval.

3 · Build one shared data foundation before adding more AI features to the app fleet

from: ClickHouse · Seagate · Cisco · DeepMind's "4 pillars"

Why it matters here: Every DeepMind-adjacent, ClickHouse, Seagate, and Cisco talk converged on the same point from different angles: AI features fail when each one has its own ad-hoc data path. With 32+ TOIC Apps Script apps already identified for the School IT Automation SaaS consolidation effort, this is the moment to design one shared, governed data layer rather than bolting AI onto each app's existing spreadsheet-backend independently.

Do next
  • Fold "shared data foundation" in as an explicit design requirement of the School IT Automation SaaS re-platforming, not an afterthought once apps are migrated.
  • For DLS-CSB's QuBE accreditation system specifically, apply DeepMind's governance-&-safety pillar (deterministic validation, auditable trails) given how compliance-sensitive accreditation data is.
Watch for
  • Each new AI feature quietly building its own private data copy or export — the "growing parallel ecosystem" risk the Publicis Groupe talk warned about directly.

4 · Name an "AI ownership ladder" now, before informal pilots outgrow their owners

from: Publicis Groupe · Woori/LG panel

Why it matters here: TOIC's app fleet has largely grown through informal, single-owner builds (often one Apps Script developer per system). The summit's "5 users → builder owns it, 50 → needs a product owner, 500 → needs a full product team" rule of thumb is a low-effort way to catch a tool before it becomes institution-critical with no formal owner or succession plan.

Do next
  • Audit current AI-touching tools (We Help chatbot, SOC/network-monitoring automation, device inventory) against actual user counts, and assign named product ownership to anything past the "50 users" line.
  • Adopt the Woori/LG panel's pairing of any AI rollout with an explicit process-redesign and role-reassignment step, not a silent bolt-on to existing duties.
Watch for
  • The single biggest bottleneck named at the summit wasn't technical — it was nobody senior being willing to "press the button" on scaling a working pilot. Make that decision-owner explicit per project, in advance.

5 · Keep tracking vendor consolidation before committing further

from: Harness/FDE-layer session

Why it matters here: The AI Roadmap already commits to Gemini as the primary API going forward, with Claude used selectively (per the earlier AI-dependency audit).
